AP https://theconversation.com/europe-is-under-increased-russian-attack-are-we-seeing-an-undeclared-war-290729 https://theconversation.com/europe-is-under-increased-russian-attack-are-we-seeing-an-undeclared-war-290729 Link copied Share article Share article Copy link Email Bluesky Facebook WhatsApp Messenger LinkedIn X (Twitter) Print article Russia’s full scale war of aggression against Ukraine has entered its fifth year. The war is stuck in a violent stalemate characterised by an escalating exchange of drone and missile attacks that target critical infrastructure and civilians in Ukraine. The conflict is also spilling out beyond the borders of the those two countries and into continental Europe more broadly in unconventional and indirect ways. Russia has been attacking European countries using what’s called “ hybrid warfare ”: the use of unconventional methods as part of a multi-domain warfighting approach. These methods aim to disrupt and disable an opponent’s actions without engaging in open hostilities. Just last month, Russia attempted drone attacks on Germany’s Leipzig Airport. The escalating, intensifying attacks on countries such as Germany and Romania amount to an undeclared war against the West, with the potential for escalation. The conflict grey zone Since the beginning of the invasion in February 2022, Russia has been attacking NATO’s European member states with a mix of tactics . These have included sabotage, assassination attempts and cyber attacks on energy grids and communication infrastructure. It has also launched physical attacks on NATO’s critical undersea cable infrastructure. These attacks were taking place below the threshold of conventional open warfare in the so-called “ grey zone of conflict ”. They were unconventional, non-attributable or falling short of physical conflict. An example of this type of conflict is the Nord Stream gas pipeline sabotage in September 2022 . This was a clandestine operation that damaged two main natural gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea and effectively put a stop to any Russian-Germany liquid gas energy business. German prosecutors blame Ukraine, but there are conflicting views on who was behind it. Russia and Belarus were accused of weaponising migrants in 2021 by opening up to the Middle East, then funnelling migrants to the borders with European Union countries. The strategy aimed to destabilise their neighbours and killed dozens of migrants. Russia has stepped up hybrid warfare operations against Europe since then. According to a recent report by the United States Congressional Research Service: the number of Russian hybrid attacks in Europe quadrupled from 2023 to 2024; another investigation compiled at least 151 incidents of reported Russian operations from February 2022 to March 2026. Read more: Explainer: what is ‘hybrid warfare’ and what is meant by the ‘grey zone’? Ratcheting up the attacks Whether it’s arson attacks against Western arms manufacturing sites or coordinated GPS jamming of Western navigation systems targeting civilian navigation and aviation , Russia is stepping up its operations. All of them have the potential to create a civilian mass casualty event. These operations still fall under the umbrella of hybrid warfare, as both deniability and lack of attribution are still key elements of Russia’s approach. But they are starting to test Western resilience. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, when addressing the Leipzig Airport incident, warned the attackers would have to “pay a price” and that Germany was increasingly becoming a target of such attacks. Germany’s government has since officially blamed Russia . Romania has also come under Russian attack. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reacted to reports of the Romanian military destroying a naval drone near one of its oil platforms in the Black Sea by calling out an “ escalating campaign of threats ” against the European Union and its critical infrastructure. This recent incident follows months of Russian drone incursions into Romanian airspace, as well as increased drone strikes close to Romania’s border. The action has affected civilians. In May 2026, a Russian drone hit an apartment building in Romania and injured two people. These incidents demonstrate Russia’s increasing willingness to openly use military force. The NATO response NATO has ramped up its air policing along its Eastern border to secure the airspace. As part of its commitment to its collective security mandate (also called Article 5), where an attack against one member is treated as an attack against all members, it has also provided more air defence capabilities to affected border states. These actions are in addition to existing NATO counters to Russian clandestine operations of sabotage and other hybrid warfare tactics. NATO’s operations Baltic Sentry , Eastern Sentry and Arctic Sentry enhance the organisation’s capability to counter Russian threats to NATO interests on land, air and sea. It seems clear the nature of Russia’s undeclared war against the West for its support of Ukraine has progressed beyond its original hybrid warfare form. NATO has increased air policing, especially around Romania, in the wake of Russian attacks. Andreea Alexandru/AP Maintaining the illusion that such Russian operations still fall below the threshold of conventional war and so do not need a more forceful response as deterrence has the potential to escalate further . NATO has to make it clear to the Kremlin that any further acts that cause civilian deaths or create large scale destruction will be regarded as an armed attack. This will in turn trigger its collective defence response. NATO leaders in the past clarified that hybrid attacks may amount to an armed attack. However, this red line is questionable given US President Donald Trump’s increased criticism of, and even hostility towards, NATO and other allies. He’s repeatedly cast doubt on the value of the collective security mandate, indicating unwillingness to defend NATO members. He also consistently downplays the Russian threat . So Russia is deliberately testing NATO’s resolve. It’s an undeclared war, with attacks intensifying. But with Trump’s commitment to the organisation doubtful, it’s hard to see how the increasingly tenuous situation progresses from here. https://baltic-review.com/zaube-wild-cul.text: Share Tweet 0 The Zaube Wild Culinary Festival connects local food with knowledge of Latvia’s natural landscape. Latvia’s relationship with the forest and the fields will take centre stage in Zaube on Saturday, 5 September, when the Zaube Wild Culinary Festival returns for its tenth edition. The free event in Zaube Manor Park, in Cēsis municipality, combines a food market, cooking demonstrations, lectures and hands-on activities around ingredients gathered from Latvia’s natural landscape. The festival is a timely expression of Latvia’s late-summer food culture. Mushrooms, berries, herbs, fish, game and preserved produce are not presented simply as seasonal commodities, but as part of a living body of knowledge passed through families and rural communities. The organisers describe this year’s theme as “Source of Strength”, inviting visitors to explore the flavours, skills and experiences that connect food with place. ([wildfoodfest.lv](https://www.wildfoodfest.lv/?utm_source=openai)) A meeting point for traditional and modern cooking The programme brings together professional chefs, home cooks, anglers, hunters, nature specialists and craftspeople. The festival’s official programme lists masterclasses led by chef Ingmārs Ladigs of Re-chef and chef Kristaps Reimanis, as well as sessions from Latvian host Māra Zemdega and demonstrations by Zaube’s hunters’ and anglers’ club. That mixture is central to the event’s character. Professional cooks can introduce new techniques, while local participants contribute recipes, preservation methods and practical knowledge about ingredients. The result is less a conventional restaurant festival than an open-air exchange between culinary expertise and rural experience. The Cēsis tourism service describes the festival as a meeting between intangible local heritage and contemporary professional cooking. It highlights traditions including the preparation of game, the collection and use of wild herbs, and the long-standing Latvian practices of mushroom and berry gathering. ([visit.cesis.lv](https://visit.cesis.lv/lielakie-pasakumi-cesu-novada-2026/?utm_source=openai)) Food as a form of local identity For small communities, events such as Zaube’s festival can do more than attract visitors for a day. They create a public setting in which local producers can explain how food is made, where ingredients come from and why particular recipes matter. The market element gives visitors an opportunity to meet makers directly, while lectures and demonstrations make the knowledge behind the products visible. One of the festival’s features this year is a presentation of “meadow meat”, connected with the Latvian Fund for Nature’s “Product of Natural Meadows” concept. According to the Cēsis tourism information, the initiative presents meat from animals fed on diverse meadow vegetation and links food quality with the maintenance of species-rich grasslands. ([visit.cesis.lv](https://visit.cesis.lv/zaubes-savvalas-kulinarais-festivals-svin-10-gadu-jubileju-ar-temu-speka-avots/?utm_source=openai)) The programme also includes a public preserving competition. Organisers invited visitors to bring a jar of their own savoury or sweet preserve, with entries judged by festival-goers for taste and appearance. It is a small but telling detail: preserving is both a practical response to the harvest season and a way of expressing household creativity. A rural event with a broader message Although the festival is rooted in Zaube, its subject reaches beyond one parish. Wild ingredients are increasingly part of conversations about regional food systems, low-waste cooking and the value of seasonal produce. The event offers those themes in an accessible form, through tasting, conversation and demonstration rather than abstract discussion. It also presents rural Latvia as a place of knowledge and experimentation. The forest is not merely scenery, and traditional food is not treated as a museum display. Both become resources for contemporary cooks, producers and visitors looking for a closer connection between landscape and everyday meals. The festival takes place from 11:00 to 17:00 in Zaube Manor Park. Entry is free. Cēsis municipality’s event listing confirms the date, while the municipality’s Amata administration lists the festival among the weekend’s public events and gives a longer operating window for the site. Visitors should check the organiser’s website for the latest programme details before travelling.
